I admit I never thought I’d do any analytical work on Resident Evil 4. Don’t get me wrong; it’s one of my favorite games. Being extremely fun to play, and a having a wonderfully creepy aesthetic are just a few of the game’s strengths. But it’s a silly game in a lot of ways. There aren’t larger messages and meanings to glean from it. And at some moments, the game mechanics and the overall story don’t match up very well. I’d like to discuss one of those moments: Luis’s famous death in castle. I’ll use this example to discuss the elements of motivation and capacity in video games.

You may recall from my previous article a discussion of a player’s motivation and capacity while playing a video game. Although I mentioned these terms, I never adequately defined them, so I’ll do so now. A player’s motivation is the reason he or she cares about playing the game and effecting some kind of difference in the world and story in which he or she is immersed. This element is present in other mediums—it’s the reason we continue to read/watch the story. A player’s capacity, unlike motivation, is intrinsically tied to game mechanics; it consists of the things that the player is able to do in the game world. The analogue of capacity in other media is simply the reader’s ability to continue to watch or read the story. There are further complexities in games, however, including that a player’s degree of capacity can effect his or her motivation, but that is a discussion for another time (probably focusing on Deus Ex). For now, recall my claim that in order for a game to be truly impactful, both of these elements must exist (or noticeably not exist, as I’ll discuss in my next article). Note also that the capacity element is harder and more important to make present, since it’s the element that video games have introduced to storytelling.

Q:

Download OS X App Store updates to update multiple Macs

I have two MacBook Airs, but I have very limited bandwidth. I would prefer to download updates once and then copy them onto all the other MacBook Airs. How can I download App Store updates once to update multiple Macs?

A:

There are two types of update.
OS X software updates are updates for the OS and OS components (e.g. iTunes). These used to be delivered through a separate software update app, but since the introduction of the Mac App Store, the OS X updates have been combined with Mac App Store updates in the Updates tab of the Mac App Store. However, the CLI tool remains, giving you more flexibility in Terminal and allow the downloading of updates without installing them, perfect for copying to other machines before the installation takes place.
You can download OS X updates without installing them (which would automatically remove them) so you can copy them, using the following command:
softwareupdate -dav

The 10.9.4 update is distributed externally, outside of the Mac App Store; the Mac App Store just provides the UI for the installation process.
Conversely, for Mac App Store apps, you need OS X Server's Caching service, as the apps are 'non-transferrable' and the app receipt must match the Apple ID that downloaded the app for the app to be updated in the future. However, if you're using the same Apple ID, or don't care about updating the app from the second machine, update the app normally then copy the .app bundle from /Applications to the other Macs as necessary.

The processes use and request different types of locks on the tables

CentOS 6.2 is old (6.2, 6 December 2011 (kernel 2.6.32-220))
HP StorageWorks MSA70 is old. (End of Life - October 2010)
HP Smart Array P800 is old. (End of Life - 2010)

So this makes me think that firmware and drivers are also old. E.g. there's no reason to run CentOS 6.2 in 2015... And I'm assuming no effort was made to keep anything current.
This also makes me think that the systems are not being monitored. Assuming HP server hardware, what did the system IML logs say? Are you running HP management agents? If not, important messages about the server and storage health could have been missed.
Did you check information from the HP Array Configuration Utility (or HP SSA)?
But in the end, you've probably suffered a port failure or expander/backplane failure:

How many SAS cables are connected to the enclosure? If 1 cable is connected, then you likely have a backplane issue because of the SAS expander in the enclosure. 
If two cables are connected, you may have a SAS cable, MSA70 controller or P800 port failure.

Your data is likely intact, but you need to isolate the issue and determine which one of the above issues is the culprit. Replacing a SAS cable is a lot easier than swapping the MSA70 controller or RAID controller card... but I guess you can get another MSA70 for $40 on eBay...

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
Post-incident review: elevated error rate on the checkout path, 12-13 September

Summary
Between 02:14 and 03:41 UTC on 13 September, approximately 6.4 percent of checkout requests failed with a gateway timeout. The impact was confined to customers in the EU region; customers routed to the US region were unaffected for the whole window. No data was lost. Customers who retried were usually successful on the second attempt, although some baskets were abandoned, and support handled 214 tickets in the window, mostly from customers asking whether their order had gone through. The incident was detected by the synthetic checkout probe at 02:19 and was resolved by rolling release 5.19.2 back to 5.19.1 at 03:41.

Timeline (all times UTC)
02:11 - release 5.19.2 completes its canary phase and is promoted to full traffic in the EU region.
02:14 - error rate on the payment authorisation endpoint begins to climb; alerting thresholds are not yet crossed.
02:19 - the synthetic probe fails twice in a row; the on-call engineer acknowledges the page.
02:26 - on-call opens the incident channel and confirms that the errors correlate with the EU deployment.
02:34 - the first hypothesis, upstream payment provider latency, is investigated and rejected; provider response times are flat.
02:47 - a second engineer observes that the connection pool for the authorisation service is exhausted, and that the pool size in the new release was reduced from 200 to 64 as part of a resource-limits change.
02:58 - decision taken to roll back rather than hot-fix, because the configuration is baked into the image.
03:12 - the rollback begins; the deployment controller drains pods one at a time.
03:41 - all EU pods are running 5.19.1 and the error rate returns to baseline.

Root cause
The resource-limits change in 5.19.2 reduced the maximum number of pooled connections per pod. Because the authorisation call is synchronous and the provider's p99 latency during the evening peak is around 400 milliseconds, the smaller pool saturated well before the CPU or memory limits were reached. Requests then queued behind the pool and the upstream load balancer timed out at two seconds. The change had been tested in staging, where traffic volume is roughly one eighth of production, so the pool never saturated there.

What went well
The synthetic probe detected the fault quickly and the rollback procedure worked as documented; the runbook was followed without improvisation and the deployment controller drained pods with no dropped requests.

What did not go well
The change to resource limits was reviewed as a routine configuration edit and did not trigger the load test that changes to application code receive. An alert on pool saturation existed but was routed to a dashboard the on-call engineer does not routinely open.

Action items
1. Add pool saturation to the paging alert set (platform, due 27 September).
2. Require a load test for any change to connection pool limits, timeouts or retry budgets (developer experience, due 4 October).
3. Document the provisioning steps for a regional rollback in the main runbook (on-call rotation).
4. Review services that reduce pool sizes outside business hours and record the accepted values in the configuration repository.
5. Add the checkout probe to the regional failover drill so it is exercised against each region separately.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Long-context holdout of well over 512 tokens in which the technical incident content sits deep in the passage rather than at the start, testing whether the register is read across a long span.

4.2 Retransmission

The client MUST set the retransmission timer when it sends a segment carrying data. If an acknowledgement covering that segment has not been received before the timer expires, the segment is retransmitted and the timer is doubled, up to a maximum of 60 seconds. A client that receives three duplicate acknowledgements SHOULD retransmit immediately without waiting for the timer.

4.3 Status register

The status register at offset 0x1F reports the current link state. Bit 0 indicates carrier detect; bit 3 is set when the receive buffer holds more than 75 percent of its capacity; bits 4 to 7 are reserved and read as zero. Writing a one to bit 9 clears the error counter. The register must be read as a single 16-bit value, since splitting the read across two accesses may return a mixture of states from consecutive samples.
